title: Rattanakosin Kingdom
capsule: The Rattanakosin Kingdom was the fourth and final era of traditional Siamese monarchy, founded in 1782 when General Chakri overthrew the short-lived Thonburi regime, crowned himself Rama I, and established Bangkok on the east bank of the Chao Phraya as the new capital. Under Rama II and Rama III the kingdom consolidated control over much of mainland Southeast Asia, absorbed Lao and Cambodian tributaries, and developed an elaborate court culture modeled on Ayutthayan precedent. The transformative reigns of Mongkut (Rama IV, r. 1851–1868) and Chulalongkorn (Rama V, r. 1868–1910) selectively modernized the administration, abolished slavery, and negotiated away peripheral territories to Britain and France to preserve the core kingdom. The absolute monarchy gave way to a constitutional revolution on 24 June 1932, ending the Rattanakosin Kingdom's political form and inaugurating the modern Thai state.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial extent is reasonably well-attested for the core Chao Phraya basin and major vassal states from administrative and treaty records; peripheral tributary boundaries in the Lao principalities and the Malay south are approximate and shift across the period.
